title: Improving mechanical and wear properties of multiphase M50 steel by tailoring bainite morphology
abstract: The martensite/bainite multiphase microstructure has shown excellent strength-toughness matching compared with the traditional martensitic microstructure. The ratio of martensite/bainite has always been the focus of performance optimization for the multiphase microstructure. However, the effect of bainite morphology on mechanical properties and wear properties remains unknown. In this work, the microstructure, mechanical, and wear properties of multiphase M50 steel with different bainite morphologies have been investigated. The austempering parameters were controlled to obtain a similar bainite fraction (around 10%) and different bainite morphologies. The microstructure characterization shows that the properly introduced lower bainite can significantly refine the lath structure due to the significant microstructure segmentation effect. When the bundle width and length of lower bainite are respectively 0.107 μm and 3.758 μm, the finest lath microstructure is obtained considering the balance of martensite growth space. The mechanical properties results show that the toughness increases without loss of strength under the tailored bainite. The high-temperature wear performance shows that the multiphase microstructure with tailored bainite results in the decrease of friction coefficient by 42% and a decline of wear loss by 37.9% due to the optimized lubrication layer. This work provides a novel perspective to further improve the mechanical and wear properties of multiphase M50 steel by finely tailoring the bainite morphology on the basis of fixed bainite content.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The bearings used in aeroengine spindle usually serve under extreme working conditions such as high temperature, high speed, and heavy load [ 1–3 ]. An excellent compressive mechanical property with a balanced combination of strength and toughness is required for the bearing steel. Due to the high hardness and dimensional stability under high temperature, the M50 steel is selected as the ideal material for the manufacturing of the bearing ring of the aeroengine [ 4 , 5 ]. The current heat treatment process for M50 steel is usually martensitic quenching followed by high-temperature tempering (QT) [ 6 , 7 ]. The microstructure obtained by this process consists of the dominant tempered martensite and a few retained austenite (RA) of less than 3%, which exhibits high strength but low toughness. As a result, it is easy to cause fatigue peeling or even fracture failure for the M50 steel treated by the traditional QT process [ 8 , 9 ].

In order to improve the strength-toughness matching, some researchers have focused on the implementation of the austempering process to obtain the martensite/bainite (M/B) multiphase microstructure for toughness improvement. Existing researches have shown that M/B multiphase microstructure obtained by austempering process is effective in improving the toughness of M50 steel [ 10 , 11 ], which could be attributed to the ultrafine M/B multiphase microstructure and higher dislocation strengthening effect. Chen et al. [ 12 ] studied the effect of bainite on the impact fracture behavior of high-strength steel with M/B multiphase microstructure. They found that the cooperation between bainite and numerous thick RA could inhibit the microcrack propagation path. In addition, Lu et al. [ 13 ] developed ultrafine M/B multiphase bearing steel with excellent toughness due to the formation of film-like RA. The above studies showed that the introduction of lower bainite could enhance the toughness from different aspects.

Although the introduction of bainite plays a positive role in toughness, the control of the bainite is critically important because of its significant impact on toughness. Therefore, researchers have focused on the regulation of the M/B multiphase microstructure by reasonably adjusting the austempering processes [ 14–17 ]. Kumar et al. [ 18 ] found that the toughness improvement could be ascribed to the fewer proportion of brittle martensite and the higher volume fraction of film-like RA after tailoring the M/B ratio. Han et al. [ 19 ] suggested that the optimized fraction of lower bainite can be obtained by applying an austempering process of 280 °C in 42CrMo steel, and then, the minimum quality loss and surface damage of wear were achieved. A recent study by Su et al. [ 20 ] indicated that higher hardness and impact toughness could be obtained in the multiphase M50 steel containing 11.9% bainite. The above analyses confirm the crucial role of bainite fraction in the multiphase microstructure. Except for the bainite volume fraction, the size and amount of bainite can be also affected by the austempering parameters [ 21 , 22 ]. In particular, under the same bainite content, the austempering parameters could exert a crucial role in changing the bainite morphology, which will influence the final performance. Yu et al. [ 23 ] significantly enhanced the hardness and wear resistance of M50 steel by modulating the nano-sized bainite (50 nm in width). Apart from this, the study concerning the effect of bainite morphology on microstructure and mechanical properties has been rarely reported.

Recently, our work shows that the best combination of strength and toughness can be obtained by controlling the volume fraction of bainite at 10%–12% in M50 steel [ 24 ]. The improvement in toughness could be ascribed to the higher density of phase boundaries, which plays a role in hindering crack propagation under impact load. In this work, for a better understanding of the effect of bainite morphology on the microstructure and properties of multiphase M50 steel, the different morphologies of bainite were obtained by adjusting austempering process based on the fixed bainite content. The influencing mechanism of bainite morphology on microstructure evolution, mechanical, and wear properties were analyzed and discussed in detail.

                         . The microstructure was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Gemini 300) and electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Nordly Max2). The SEM specimens were polished and soaked in a 4% volume fraction of nitric acid alcohol solution for 5 min. Meanwhile, the numbers of bainite at the same magnification of the view fields are also counted by Photoshop software. The EBSD specimens were electropolished and scanned with 0.05 μm step size. sections.heading: Mechanical properties and wear tests
paragraphs:
The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) was tested by a universal testing machine (SUNS WDW-50). The specimens with a gauge length of 15 mm ( Fig. 1 
                         . (a)) were subjected to the room temperature tensile process at 1 mm/min. After the test, the fracture morphology was observed by SEM after ultrasonic cleaning. The standard Charpy un-notch specimens with dimensions of 5 × 10 × 55 mm (GB/T 229–2007) were tested using a drop hammer impact toughness tester (Wance 452D-4) at room temperature. In each condition, three specimens were tested to obtain the average value and error bar.

The wear resistance was tested by a high-temperature wear tester (HT-1000) based on ASTM Standard G99-95 [ 25 ]. Before the test, the surfaces of the wear specimens were mechanically ground and polished. In this test, a ceramic ball (Si 3 N 4 ), a common ball bearing roller, was used as a friction pair on the surface of the specimen as shown in  Fig. 1 . (b). The wear tests at 300 °C were conducted at 600 r/min with a constant load of 20 N. During the test, the friction coefficients were recorded during the 120 min of wear. After the test, the quality loss was recorded, and then the surface morphology of wear scars was observed by SEM.

Fig. 4 
                          shows the schematic diagram of the heat treatment processes. The specimens were initially heated to 1090 °C and lasted for 1 h, followed by the salt bath with different temperatures and times. After that, the specimens were subjected to oil quenching to obtain martensite. Finally, these quenched specimens were conducted to a tempering process at 540 °C for 2 h in an air furnace and repeated three cycles. Additionally, another group (QT) was subjected to standard martensitic quenching and tempering.  Table 2 
                          lists the specific parameters of the heat treatment processes. After precisely tailoring the austempering temperature and time, the volume fraction of bainite is controlled at about 10%.

sections.heading: Microstructure of as-quenched specimens
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                             shows the microstructure of quenched and tempered specimens. The microstructure of the as-quenched specimen A mainly consists of martensite/austenite (M/A) island and a few undissolved carbides (UC). For the as-quenched specimens with multiphase structure, there are a few bainite bundles (B) inside the prior austenite grain.  Table 3 
                             shows the statistical results of the average length, width, and number of bainite bundles. It is clear that with the increase of austempering temperature, the width, and the number of bainite increases, while the length of bainite distinctly decreases. This demonstrates that the bainite morphology can be effectively tailored through the adjustment of austempering parameters. Increasing the austempering time can lead to the elongation of the bainite, while more and wider bainite will be obtained under the higher austempering temperature.

Fig. 6 
                             shows XRD patterns and volume fractions of RA for the as-quenched specimens. It can be seen that the volume fraction of RA is 20.6% in specimen A, which is less than the M/B multiphase specimens. This phenomenon may be caused by the increase of austenite carbon content induced by carbon partitioning during the austempering process. The more carbon contained in the austenite, the more difficult the martensitic transformation is [ 4 ]. Thus, there is more carbon content in the austempered specimens. It should be also noted that the volume fraction of RA in specimen D reaches 32.9%, while the volume fraction of RA in other M/B multiphase specimens ranges from 22% to 28%. It is known that the larger bainite/austenite interface will provide more diffusion channels for the carbon partition from bainite to adjacent austenite. On the other hand, the higher number of bainite can undoubtedly contribute to the carbon partition process. Conclusively, it can be assumed that the comprehensive effect of length and number of bainite results in more carbon content, so that the highest amount of RA is achieved in specimen D.

sections.heading: Microstructure of as-tempered specimens
paragraphs:
Fig. 7 
                             shows the SEM microstructure of the tempered specimens. Compared with specimen A, the microstructure of M/B multiphase specimens is finer. It should be also noted that the size of the precipitated carbide (PC) is distinctly smaller than specimen A, which could be caused by promoting effect of higher phase interface density for carbide nucleation [ 11 ]. In the austempered specimens, there are still large-sized M/A islands in specimen F, demonstrating the differences in refining effect for the M/B multiphase microstructure. On the contrary, the nano-scale M/A islands are observed in specimen D, which means that the small-sized RA blocks are generated during the tempering for specimen D.

The TEM microstructure of the as-tempered specimens is shown in  Fig. 8 
                            . The microstructure of specimen D is illustrated in  Fig. 8 . (a), where it can be seen that the M/B laths were located in the matrix in different directions with plenty of thin-filmed RA around.  Fig. 8 . (b) depicts the microstructure of specimen F. Obviously, the lath width and the RA thickness of specimen F are larger than that of specimen D.

Fig. 9 
                             shows the inverse pole figures (IPF) of tempered microstructure obtained by different processes. Consistent with SEM observation ( Fig. 7 .), the austempered specimens exhibit the finer lath, as compared with QT specimens. The average size of the lath is the smallest in specimen D (0.772 μm), while the average size of the lath is the largest in specimen F (0.915 μm). This result confirms that the bainite morphology would exert an important effect in the microstructure refinement, though similar bainite fractions (about 10%) are obtained for the austempered specimens.

The pole figures and texture analysis of specimens A, D, and F are shown in  Fig. 10 
                            . It can be found that specimen A exhibits two main types of textures, including cube {001}<110> and copper {112}<211> textures. The specimens with the M/B multiphase microstructure show the brass R {111}<110> texture. Since the brass R {111}<110> texture has a higher number of variants than that of cube {001}<110> and copper {112}<211> textures [ 31 ], the existence of brass R {111}<110> texture could improve the toughness of the steel by improving the ability to slip deformation [ 32 ].

Fig. 11 
                             shows XRD patterns and the dislocation density of α-Fe in the tempered specimens. From the calculated dislocation densities, it is observed that the dislocation density of specimen A reaches 5.2 × 10 15 , which is significantly lower than that of all the austempered specimens. Additionally, the highest dislocation density is detected in specimen D (10.2 × 10 15 ). It has been reported that the decomposition of RA can lead to the generation of dislocations and micro-strain in the surrounding ferrite packet to accommodate the transformation strain [ 33 ]. In this work, it can be assumed that the more RA content in specimen D illustrated in  Fig. 6 . (b) could be the main reason for the higher dislocation density.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties of tempered specimens are shown in  Fig. 12 
                         . The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of specimen D increases from 2451.8 MPa to 2611.8 MPa, as compared with specimen A, while the lowest UTS is observed in specimen F (2271.7 MPa). From  Fig. 12 . (b), compared with specimen A (55.4 J), a significant improvement in impact absorption energy is achieved for all multiphase specimens, in which the highest impact absorption energy is shown in specimen D (93.2 J). It can be concluded that the bainite morphology exerts a crucial influence on mechanical properties in the multiphase M50 steel. The best match of strength and toughness can be obtained in specimen D with the finest lath microstructure ( Fig. 9 .).

The tensile fracture morphology of specimens A and D is shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . As shown in  Fig. 13 . (a) and (d), the width of the fiber region in specimen D (16.9 μm) is wider than that of specimen A (11.6 μm). Besides, the flat fracture surface can be seen in the center of specimen A, while the large plastic deformation is observed in the fracture center of specimen D. From  Fig. 13 . (b) and (e), the fracture fringes of specimen A are relatively straight, while the fracture fringe is curved and staggered in specimen D. This indicates the higher ability to resist crack propagation for specimen D. Furthermore, the local high-magnification of fracture morphology is presented in  Fig. 13 . (c) and (f)), where it can be seen that specimens A and D both exhibit the quasi-cleavage fracture characteristics. However, as compared with specimen A, a smaller area of cleavage plane and a higher number of dimples can be observed in specimen D. The wider fiber region, curved fracture fringe and higher number of dimples together prove that the fracture characteristic of specimen D tends to ductile fracture.

sections.heading: Wear properties
paragraphs:
The evolution of friction coefficients as a function of testing time is shown in  Fig. 14 
                         . The fluctuation of friction coefficients can be found in the initial period of wear before reaching a stable wear stage. This phenomenon may be due to the fact that the specimens have to experience a running period to match the wear scars with the friction pair [ 34 ]. Compared with the friction coefficient of specimen A (about 0.7), the friction coefficients of the M/B multiphase specimens show a significant reduction and maintain a smoothly decreasing trend during the wear process. In addition, the lowest friction coefficient is obtained in specimen D (about 0.4).

The SEM images of the wear scars of specimens A, D, and F are shown in  Fig. 15 
                         . The obvious grooves caused by the ploughing effect [ 35–37 ] can be detected on the wear scars of specimens A, D, and F. The deepest ploughing grooves can be observed in specimen A. Meanwhile, there is significant heterogeneity in the widths of the grooves in specimens A and F. The big peeling pits can be also observed on the ploughing grooves. This should be attributed to the severe deformation of specimens A and F after being ploughed by debris. Compared with specimens A and F, shallow and uniform ploughing grooves can be found in specimen D, and the wear scar is also smoother. In addition, the peeling pits can be observed on the ploughing grooves for specimens A and F. This demonstrates the stable wear process in specimen D, which is well coincided with the friction coefficient results in  Fig. 14 .

The quality loss of specimens for the wear tests at 300 °C is shown in  Fig. 16 
                         . It can be seen that the quality of wear for the specimens decreases with the reduction of the friction coefficient ( Fig. 14 .). Compared with specimen A (16.8 mg), significant declines in quality loss are achieved for all multiphase specimens, in which the lowest quality loss is acquired in specimen D (10.6 mg). It can be inferred that specimen D was subjected to minimal cutting force due to the smoother abrasion marks ( Fig. 15 . (b)). Unlike the M/B multiphase specimens, specimen A exhibited a larger wear quality loss.

sections.heading: Effect of bainite morphology on the microstructure
paragraphs:
To clarify the mechanism of the microstructure refinement under different bainite morphologies, the microstructure evolution during the austempering and martensitic quenching is analyzed in  Fig. 17 
                         . Bainite can not only provide additional nucleation sites at the phase interface for subsequent martensite formation, but also the separation of prior austenite induced by bainite can limit the growth range and size of martensite [ 24 ]. It is easy to understand that the lath structure of austempered specimens (specimens B, D, and F) would be finer than that of specimens treated by single martensitic quenching (specimen A). In addition, insignificant separating effects appear in specimens B and F. In specimen B, though the length of bainite is relatively longer (4.73 μm long) which could provide more nucleation sites, the smaller amount of bainite will also lead to excessive growth space of subsequent martensite transformation. For specimen F, the size of bainite is coarser (2.97 μm long) due to higher austempering temperature, which will result in fewer nucleation sites of subsequent martensite formation. Therefore, based on the similar bainite fraction, the best microstructure refining effect would be achieved in specimen D due to the reasonable size (3.76 μm long) and quantity of bainite, which exhibits a significant reduction in the average lath size by 13.5% ( Fig. 9 (D) ) compared with specimen A. In summary, the bainite morphology that is optimized for microstructure refinement is that the average length of the bainite laths is greater than 3.8 μm and sufficient quantity.

sections.heading: Effect of bainite morphology on the mechanical property
paragraphs:
Under the special bainite morphology (3.76 μm long and 52.4 per 100 μm 2 ), a large amount of RA is retained in the quenched specimen D due to the longer time for carbon diffusion ( Fig. 7 . (b)). The RA will be decomposed during the subsequent tempering, thus resulting in the expansion volume and dislocation generation [ 38 ]. As a result, more dislocations will arise from the volume changes during the tempering of specimen D ( Fig. 11 . (b)), which would be beneficial to the tensile strength [ 39 ]. Meanwhile, the average lath of specimen D is finer than that of other specimens due to the significant grain segmentation effect. Consequently, the precipitation of nano carbides will be accelerated for the increasing density of phase interface [ 11 ], which should intensify the secondary hardening effect for specimen D [ 40 ]. In addition, the refined RA can improve the impact toughness of specimens by delaying the initiation and propagation of microcracks [ 41 ]. Thus, the higher impact toughness of specimen D should be attributed to the refinement of laths ( Fig. 9 . (d)) and small size RA ( Fig. 7 . (c)). In addition, the martensite lath size can be regarded as the equivalent grain size and conforms to the Hall-Petch formula:

(d)), the highest strength can be expected for specimen D. Numerous studies have shown that the impact toughness of M/B multiphase steel is closely associated to the size of the lath and RA [ 45 ]. The density of interfaces would be higher for the specimens with finer lath, which means that the longer the crack propagation needs to bypass [ 43 , 46 ]. Therefore, the higher impact energy would be absorbed for the specimens with finer lath size [ 44 ]. In summary, a certain length of bainite bundles (more than 3.7 μm in length) and sufficient amount of bainite (more than 52 per 100 μm 2 ) is the key to the increase of strength and toughness for M/B multiphase M50 steel. By tailoring the bainite morphology within a suitable range, the most significant microstructure refinement effect will be achieved. The increase of dislocation density, refinement of the carbide and lath size will together contribute to the tensile strength. In addition, the refinement of the lath and RA should be responsible for the significant increase of impact toughness.

sections.heading: Effect of bainite morphology on the wear property
paragraphs:
Fig. 18 
                          shows the wear mechanism of specimens D and F. The surface of the specimens will be subject to a serious ploughing effect caused by large deformation and peeling off from the surface layer ( Fig. 15 .) [ 47 ]. During the break-in period, the large-size hard phase dominated by primary carbides is exposed to the top of the matrix in specimen F. After that, the exposed carbides of specimen F are subjected to cyclic compressive stress and cyclic shear stress from the ceramic ball, and then, nucleation and initiation of the microcracks under the surface layer of specimen F are caused predominantly by the stress concentration and dislocation accumulation. On the contrary, the tensile strength of specimen D is greatly increased under the unique bainite morphology (3.76 μm in length and 0.11 μm in width). Meanwhile, a higher density of phase boundaries was obtained in specimen D, which indicates that more barriers need to cross in the way of dislocation slip [ 48 ]. Thus, there is less probability for microcracks to nucleate and grow in the finer microstructure, which radically improves the wear resistance. Furthermore, the highest strength will also play a key role in protecting the matrix from the flattest plowing for specimen D. In this work, coincided with the above analysis, there are fewer peeling pits for specimen D ( Fig. 15 . (b)) with the finest lath size. Therefore, it can be concluded that finer microstructure and higher dislocation density can be achieved by the finely regulation of bainite with sufficient length and adequate number of bundles, which together contribute to the decrease of the friction coefficients and wear quantity for specimen D.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In this work, to further optimize the bainite structure in multiphase M50 steel, the different morphology of bainite were designed and then obtained by adjusting austempering process on the basis of optimization of bainite content. The influencing mechanism of bainite morphology on microstructure evolution, mechanical, and wear properties was analyzed and discussed in detail. The following conclusions can be drawn. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            After controlling the bainite fraction at about 10%, the difference in bainite morphology would exert an important effect on the quenched and tempered microstructure. When the bainite is tailored to a reasonable size (0.107 μm in width and 3.758 μm in length), a higher amount of RA is obtained after quenching. In addition, the most significant refinement in lath size is achieved after tempering, which shows a decreasing trend from 0.892 to 0.772 μm compared with the traditional QT process. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The mechanical property results of tempered specimens indicate that the excellent matching of strength and toughness can be obtained under the finely tailored bainite morphology, in which the toughness is increased by 68.2% while the strength is increased by 6.5%. However, the bainite with lower length and higher width (obtained at higher austempering temperature) will lead to deterioration of properties in multiphase specimens. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            When the bainite morphology is finely tailored, both the friction coefficient and wear quality are reduced due to the shallower plowing groove in the higher strength of the matrix. In addition, the number of peeling pits significantly decreases because of the hindering effect of higher boundary density on crack extension.

In summary, this study discovers the crucial role of bainite morphology in the microstructure, mechanical, and wear properties. As well, a reasonable bainite morphology was obtained to achieve improved strength-toughness properties and wear resistance. The results obtained in this work will provide a new idea for the design and optimization of multiphase M50 steel.
